> Q5: "The negative result shows LLMs can't introspect" why do you think this might be? Is it a training data issue, architectural limitation, or something about how RLHF works? Do you have hypotheses for what would enable introspection?"

That’s a good question. We believe it is a mixture of training and architecture. In training, the LLM has probably sometimes seen the format of giving multiple outputs (hence it acts according to that format when prompted to output multiple outputs), but apparently never linked this type of list generation to the internal distribution it has, thus giving an answer that has the right format but not the right content. This might be because content is harder to get right than format. We have qualitatively observed that list-generation in an auto-regressive manner might derail the distribution: The LLM is not talking about the distribution about the initial question, but conditioned on the options it already listed. This is similar to an observation made by Zheng et al., 2025. They explicitly build a mechanism that blacks out the attention to previous generated options. They claim that this is a way to train this into the LLM. Hence, it might be a combination of training data and the training loss / design. We hope that the SelfReflect benchmark allows future papers to explore these hypotheses quantitatively.

> Q6: How does your Sample & Summarize approach compare to existing methods like Semantic Entropy (Farquhar et al. 2024), which also clusters sampled answers? What's the advantage of natural language output over numerical entropy?

We see sample & summarize as similar in spirit to semantic entropy (SE), in that both try to convey how many answer options there are. The bigger difference is the output format: SE produces a number whereas sample & summarize produces a string. While SE can thus be evaluated with classical scores like AUROC, we require the SelfReflect score to pivot into the evaluation of strings that summarize uncertainties. 

About the advantage of strings over numerical uncertainty outputs: We see strings as the next step in uncertainty quantification for LLMs. Providing numerical uncertainties (and making them faithful) was the first step, mirroring how uncertainties have been communicated in computer vision and classification. But we believe LLMs can go beyond this: A number alone reveals to some extent how certain an LLM is, but many users implicitly use a threshold at something like 50% to decide whether to trust the LLM. With a full text that tells not only about which parts of the answer the LLM is unsure, but also which other options it deems likely, the user gets a much more detailed and honest insight into the knowledge state of the LLM. Outside user-interaction, such strings can also be the starting point for the LLM to refine its answer. Once it has verbalized its uncertainty, it can launch lookups, tool uses, or follow-up questions to the user to better refine its knowledge (whereas a number would only enable it to decide not to answer, or maybe to allocate more reasoning budget, but without direction). For a reasoning model, we see this as a missing building block; currently even frontier reasoning models get stuck in one reasoning path. Overall, we thus believe that giving an honest description of uncertainties as a string is the required stepping stone to enabling new capabilities in both user interaction and reasoning. We see it as our objective in the uncertainty quantification community to develop this building block.

Thank you for providing the InfoSumm baseline. We agree it is similar in nature (a masked-out task intended to measure the PMI between summary and document), though different in the exact estimator, making it interesting to compare against. We have implemented it, with exact details in the new Appendix F.9 and a general discussion in our related works section on summarization. To test it against SelfReflect, we follow the experimental setup of Section 4.1, measuring how often it assigns good summaries better scores than (different kinds of) bad summaries. We report the findings below and in the revised version of the paper. We find that InfoSumm is able to tell apart Good vs bad, but none of the more challenging pairs of summaries. In fact, it prefers summaries that only mention the most likely answer over those that mention all options, similar to the SR-PMI baseline that uses a similar estimator. Note also that besides InfoSumm, we provide two other summarization-specific baselines: The “Summarization” baseline in tables 1, 2, 3 uses consistency, fluency, relevance, and coherence ratings, which are the standard in summarization literature, and LM Judge is prompted to judge the quality of the summary string in one go.

What our theorem state is that:

i. [the if part =>] If statement 1 turns out to be true, then statement 2 must be true, AND

ii. [the only if part <=] if statement 2 turns out to be true, then statement 1 must be true.

The intuition is that under our graphical model, the ability of a summary $S$ to hold the same amount of information about a new sample $B$ as the samples $A^{(1:N)}$ turns out to be equivalent to the conditional probability of the new sample $B$ given either the samples $A^{(1:N)}$ or their summary $S$ being equal.
Appendix A.2 provides a proof of why this holds for our graphical model. 

So, we are not saying that “conditional probability is being measured by mutual information”; in fact, in general, such equality doesn’t hold. However, in our graphical model of Figure 2, if one of the equalities about conditional probability or mutual information holds, then the other must also hold. 
We hope this clarifies the confusion. Please let us know if you need further explanation!

> W4: Could you please explain why we should use 1-Wasserstein distance to measure the difference between distributions instead of JS/KL divergence?

Indeed we find that SelfReflect is robust to the choice of the exact distance, as long as it is over the whole vocabulary logit vector. For example, replacing Wasserstein distance with KL distance leads to virtually identical results. We choose the Wasserstein over the KL distance because it generalizes gracefully to settings in which we only have the top-1 word, like in blackbox judge models, in which is reduces to an accuracy (we hinted at this in footnote 2, and have now expanded the explanation in the revised version, highlighted in blue). 

This graceful generalization is related to the capability of (1-)Wasserstein distance to provide a finite and meaningful measure of divergence in two distributions even when the distributions may have zero or little overlap in their support. In such cases, KL-divergence may explode and need to be capped and JS-divergence may return almost flat metric values which carry no meaningful signal to indicate how much the involved distributions differ.  

When we use even simpler distances, like comparing only the log likelihood of the true masked word instead of the whole vector, we observe drops in performance (this is the PR-logl baseline in Tables 1-3).

> W1: I am not sure that the authors effectively justify why a natural language summary of the answer distribution is better than just teaching the model to generate structured output representing is answer distribution: something like [("Paris", 0.75), ("Marseille", 0.15), ("Toulouse", 0.10)].

Thanks to its rigorous information-theoretic foundations, SelfReflect should continue to serve its purpose in those more complex cases as well.

> Q3: I would want to see some discussion of if these summaries are actually helpful for an end-user. There is no rigorous discussion of whether distribution summaries in natural language are actually useful, and what the benefit is compared to other ways to summarize the distribution of answers from an LLM.

We know that measures of uncertainty can be useful to end-users for establishing trust (e.g., Zhang et al 2020). However, existing measures of uncertainty in the form of numbers have empirically been shown to perform suboptimally at this task (see Corvelo Benz and Rodriguez, 2024, and references therein). One argument is that this is because looking at the probability of the most likely answer loses information about the full distribution (Yona et al, 2022). Another is the fact that humans are, on average, not good at interpreting numeric expressions of probability (e.g., Sanborn and Chater, 2016; Tversky and Kahneman, 1983). Natural language summaries of distributions can address both of these issues.

While a full user study on the uncertainties for human-AI collaborative pipelines is beyond the scope of this work, we provide a user study on our SelfReflect score, where raters have a high inter-rater correlation, indicating that users have a consistent understanding of how well a summary captures a distribution.

One can view semantic clustering as one part of the task an LLM needs to do while generating a summary string, see also the response to your question about semantic entropy below. 

However, in this paper we do not dive too much into the clustering direction, because clustering is often understood as “Given K clusters, find representatives and assignments, usually based on embeddings”. Our perspective on the problem does not use this setup and comes from a more general information-theory perspective: What information (in the form of a summary string) does one need to communicate such that it triggers the same downstream understanding in an LLM judge / user that another information (in the form of a distribution of strings) would trigger? This is the original motivation of our work, and the theoretical basis for section 3. We compare this to related work in summarization, because it is very close to both the higher-level idea of compression and also to some specific, mathematical proposals in that field (measuring mutual information via a downstream task).

We would like to thank you for your review on our paper in which we explore a new frontier for uncertainty communication in LLMs. We respond to your questions below.

> W1: To be honest, I am not quite familiar with this area but would like to ask a very general question. Why do you think the topic, whether a LLM can accurately express its own confidence through natural language, is important?

Firstly, we believe that accurate uncertainty quantification is important for LLMs. If a model appears confident when it is actually uncertain, this can lead to false reliance on uncertain information, and distrust in LLMs’ outputs. 

Second, we believe natural language expression of uncertainty is a richer, and more interpretable, way of conveying distributional uncertainty than existing UQ methods for LLMs. Most of these existing methods output a confidence in a single answer (e.g., verbalized confidence approaches), or provide a single number that conveys the amount of uncertainty in the answer distribution (e.g., semantic entropy). This is a natural first step in UQ for LLMs, and mirrors how uncertainties have been communicated in computer vision and classification.

We believe LLMs can go beyond this. Unless the model has no uncertainty, or it is a simple yes/no question, any single number is necessarily a lossy expression of the model’s distribution over responses. For example, providing simply the probability that a single answer is correct doesn’t tell us anything about how many other options the LLM considers plausible, much less why it is uncertain about the answer. This information can be expressed in natural language, however. When given such a natural-language expression of uncertainty, the user (or the LLM) can look to external tools to refine the distribution (for example, by looking up additional information that could rule in or out possibilities). 

> W2: Based on W1, do we even have a promising metric to reflect LLM’s internal probability distribution yet? If not, the topic of investigating whether a LLM can accurately express its internal probability distribution may not be reliable.

This is an interesting question. We define the LLM’s internal probability distribution as the generative distribution over answers $Q(a|c)$ that the LLM generates given some context, if prompted many times. Existing work (e.g., Kadavath et al 2022; Zhu et al 2024; Nakkiran et al 2025) suggests that, in many cases, this sampling distribution approximates the true data distribution $P(a|c)$. Further, $Q(a|c)$ is, by definition, a distribution that the LLM has information about and should be able to summarize.
We note that, while we focus on approximating $Q(a|c)$ in the paper, the SelfReflect metric can be used to evaluate distance to *any* probability distribution that we have samples from. On a mathematical level, the SelfReflect score is a distance between the information of an arbitrary string and an arbitrary distribution of strings. If future authors wish to evaluate distance to some alternative distribution (e.g., the true data distribution, if it is available), the SelfReflect score is a good choice. 

> W3: For Eq2, I am quite confused why the left hand side is equivalent to the right hand side? Why is the conditional probability measured by mutual information?

Thank you for your question. Equation 2 of the paper refers to Proposition 3.1, which is a theorem whose complete formulation and proof are provided in Theorem A.1 of Appendix A.2. We want to provide an intuition below.

The way to understand Proposition 3.1 is as follows.  Under the given graphical model provided in Figure 2 [same as Figure 5 in Appendix A], consider the following two statements:  

Statement 1: The information content about a new sample $B$ in given samples $A^{(1:N)}$ is equal to the information content about the same new sample $B$ in the summary $S$ of these samples. 

Statement 2: The conditional probability of a new sample $B$ given $A^{(1:N)}$ is equal to the conditional probability of the same sample $B$ given the summary $S$ of these samples.

We would like to thank you for coming back, and for your positive reception of our rebuttal experiments so far. We are happy to offer more experiments below to address your last questions.

> W2.1: While I agree with the authors rationale for good vs almost good samples, I am not fully convinced in the means of obtaining them. There are several iterations of model generated examples which is inherently complex and may require a whole separate work to analyze its robustness (even though they are well documented in the paper).

To study the robustness of our experiment setup in Table 1, we have now also added almost-good summaries that are generated in a one-step process. So instead of first deriving a good summary and then changing it into an almost-good one, we now directly generate an almost-good summary by providing the sample distribution. You can find the results below (on Natural Questions and Qwen 2.5 7B in this case). 

They agree with what we report in the paper: Most baseline metrics are able to distinguish a good from an almost-good summary in 72% to 94% of the cases. SelfReflect is more fine-grained and can distinguish, in this dataset, every single good summary from their mid counterpart (this one-step way of generating almost-good summaries seems to make them slightly easier to distinguish than adapting the good summary as we do in the main experiments). Note also that besides this ablation, we also have an ablation where humans write good and almost-good summaries in Appendix G, Table 9, with agreeing results. With these agreeing results under the ablated experimental setups, we are quite certain about the robustness of our findings.

> W2.2.3: Indeed, I agree that reasoning models are generalists even though they are trained for math problems. At the same time, the models specifically trained for summarization might be more capable in producing summaries.

We believe we should further clarify the nuance about the promise of the reasoning models!
Sorry for a long explanation, but we feel it’s beneficial for the sake of explanation if we are explicit and comprehensive here.

Producing a good summary of the model's internal uncertainties basically requires two components: 1) Being able to list out or be in some sense aware of the different possible options in the internal distribution, and 2) summarizing them into a consistent answer.
The motivation for evaluating the reasoning models is the potential promise (which we formed based on our qualitative observations about their behavior of the kind exemplified with Qwen3-32B in our previous response) that, unlike the non-reasoning models, the reasoning-models might have an ability to use their reasoning-block to "brainstorm" different possible answers in a way that coincides with their probability distribution when drawing independent samples (which is the reference for the SelfReflect score). This would imply that the reasoning-models might perform significantly better in terms of producing a single-decoding summary of their predictive distribution, because they perform better at the first component above.
This is evaluated with prompt "Basic" of Table 4, which for reasoning models is denoted as "Reasoning" in Table 5. You can see the exact prompt in the example with Qwen3-32B in our earlier response.
Surprisingly, we found that the SelfReflect scores for the Reasoning method for reasoning-models were worse than for the Basic method for non-reasoning-models. The reasoning block often comes up with different options than the model actually thinks of, failing at component 1.

The second component, summarizing given options, seems to work consistently across models, including reasoning models. Our results suggest that the performance of Sample&Summarize method for reasoning models are about as good as non-reasoning, e.g. compare Sample&Summarize numbers for Qwen-2.5-32B vs DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-2.5-32B: for N=10, 91 vs 91, and for N=20, 91 vs 90, respectively. These results suggest that the summarization component alone is not a bottleneck in the process. (Note: for “summarization component”, the options to be summarized are provided in context here, in contrast to the Basic/Reasoning prompt, where the model has to reflect on and summarize the different options in one decoding step).

We would like to thank the reviewer for the detailed review and the enthusiasm about our work on this new frontier of uncertainty communication. We respond to the questions below.

> W1. Controlled experiments in section 4 concern different models, raising questions about the generalization of the results (see Questions). 

In section 4, we test whether our SelfReflect benchmark score works across multiple models, both when using the models as judges and when judging the distributions of those models. We do this to test the robustness of our method. We did not test every combination of models due to limitations of our compute availability and the feasible amount of human annotation & quality-assurance (sections 4.1 and 4.3). Please see our answers to your questions below.

> W2. Some sections are a bit confusing or not clearly explained (see Questions for details)

Thank you for the feedback, we updated the paper to address your feedback, and uploaded a new revision (changes are in blue). We hope that our changes resolve any inclarity. We go into detail in the questions below.

> Q1: I’m curious to understand how the definition of an ideal summary would account for cases where some of the answers have uncertainty in themselves, e.g., “It’s likely to be Paris” or “It’s possible that the answer is Toulouse”?

This is an interesting question. Our metric bases on predictive sufficiency, i.e., a summary is ideal if, when given to an LLM judge, the LLM judge will predict the same way it would predict as when given the distribution of answers. When the answers in the distribution contain hedging statements themselves, it depends on how the LLM judge interprets them when filling in the masked-out tasks. We have observed that LLMs (judges) implicitly assign distributions to statements like “It’s likely”. For example, when prompting Qwen 2.5 7B with “Most likely A, but could be B or C”, and then asking to choose one of them in a SelfReflect-style masked-out task, it produces 50% A, 25% B, 25% C. So models generate quite reasonable logits for masked-out tokens even when conditioned with context containing “It’s likely…” etc. The ideal summary would need to make the LM judge output the same distribution, i.e., it would need to reflect the same uncertainties. 

> Q2: I was interested in knowing how exactly Self-Reflect compares to other baselines such as LLM-as-a-judge in some controlled experiment similar to study 1 in Section 4.1. Can the authors comment on whether there’s a minimum number of samples to ensure the faithfulness of SelfReflect (i.e., if we have less than N sampling budget, we’re better off using other baseline metric?)

Thank you for the suggestion! In Appendix B, we ablate both the number of answers in the reference distribution (in the judge context) and the number of answers that we use for our MC estimation (the number of masked-out tasks). We now added an experiment where we keep the reference distribution constant (and thus equal to the context provided to the baselines), and only vary the number of answers we calculate the masked-out tasks over, from 1 answer to 50 answers (our default). We report results for Qwen 2.5 7B on Natural Questions and all baselines below and add them to the paper in Appendix B.2. The performance is kept up from n=50 down to n=5, allowing to save compute budget. At n=2 and n=1, performance starts to decrease slightly, especially on harder cases like good vs almost-good and percentage vs or-concatenated, but stays above that of the baselines. Note that this was not the case in Appendix B; when reducing the answers _in the reference distribution / context_ down to 1 the metric becomes unfaithful by design (it is better to report the greedy answer). Reducing only the number of samples in the masked-out tasks is thus a better way to save on compute budget while staying faithful, thank you for suggesting the experiment!

We would like to thank the reviewer for the detailed review and the interesting questions. We respond to the questions below.

> W1: Antropomorphising language (interal beliefs, making LLMs aware of their internal uncertainties, all options it deems possible)

Thank you for the remarks. We in no way intend to antropomorphise the LLMs we test; we see them as mathematical object, in particular as distributions over strings. We have chosen these terms due to brevity and to make the sometimes rather technical content easier to understand. To prevent misunderstandings, we have added an explanatory footnote in the revised version (changes are highlighted in blue). 

> W2.1: Empirical benefits are unclear. The Tab. 1 presents comparison between several metrics as well as ablations of the SelfReflect. It can be seen that in Good vs Bad summaries the LM Judge is only second to the unablated SelfReflect, and even then 0.01% away from not achieving 95% significance

It is correct that LM Judge is able to tell apart good from bad summaries, like most other baselines and SelfReflect. However, note that the good vs bad case is only a very rough first sanity check. Bad summaries change major content in the summary, mentioning wildly different answers than the LLM actually gives. The more interesting summary pairs are the finer-grained ones like good vs almost-good, percentage vs or-concatenated, etc. We want a benchmark metric to give a better score to a summary that mentions all possibilities rather than just the majority one, and similarly, when presented with two (already very good) summaries that either give all possibilities or all possibilities plus their (correct) percentages, we want the benchmark metric to reward the latter. To make a longer-shot comparison, the generative vision field is shifting away from Frechet distance based on Inception embeddings (FID) towards using Frechet distance based on DINOv2 embeddings (FD-DINOv2), because the former could not tell apart subtle quality differences of strong models anymore. Benchmark metrics require this fine-grained precision to reliably measure progress in the field, and we found that only SelfReflect is able to detect those differences in fine-grained pairs like good vs almost-good, whereas all baseline metrics collapse to close to random performance. This effect is significant and robust across all tested datasets and models.

> W2.1 (cont): Tab.1 could be presented as a heatmap as well, depicting the performance for all combinations of summaries incorporating all pairs for a more wholesome picture. 

We intentionally do not show all combinations of summary pairs for two reasons. First, the summaries are computed on different subsplits of the dataset. Good-vs-bad and good-vs-almost-good are computed on the full dataset. Detailed-vs-truncated is only computed on questions where the answers in the answer distribution are all semantically the same, but have varying levels of details. Verbalized-vs-majority etc are computed only on questions where the answer distribution covers multiple answers but those answers are all of the same level of detail. We do this to control for confounders, which allows us to study these two aspects in isolation. We could thus only show all-combinations within each dataset split, but it would make the results harder to understand because they would become three-dimensional (summary 1 vs summary 2 vs benchmark metric) and sparse (due to the data splits). We find the 2D table easier to interpret, since it covers all important comparisons already. We will however highlight the table in heatmap-like colors in the revised version, thank you for the suggestion!

> W2.2.1: The data for the Tab. 1 was reportedly created by using Qwen2.5 7B for answer generation and Gemini 2.0 Flash for summary creation. Given the tiny margins for the main Good vs Bad summaries experiment, one may want to ablate this by answers and summaries coming from different models / generated by other means. The almost-good summary generation appears to be even less robust, since it is created starting from an already model generated summary. The other pairings also seem somewhat arbitrary. 

We have conducted these ablations. In Appendix D, Table 7, we report a cross-table of different LLM Judges and LLMs whose answer distributions are summarized (Llama, Qwen, Phi). In Appendix G, Table 8, we use human-written summaries instead of Gemini 2.0 Flash-generated ones. Our findings are robust across all of these experiments. As explained above, the margins are very solid in all experiments on the finer-grained testcases.

summary.value:
The authors introduce SelfReflect, a novel metric to measure the faithfulness of LLMs expressing their uncertainty about answers. Specifically, they examine a certain type of expression of uncertainty, which entails an explicit natural language "description" of a distribution. The SelfReflect metric is a method to measure the consistency between such a natural language "distribution summary" and the real output distribution of the LLM. They do this by alternating putting the distribution summary or some real samples of the distribution in the context and seeing how the distribution of a masked word changes in these two scenarios. The logic: if conditioning on the distribution summary and the "real distribution" (represented by a set of samples) leads to similar masked word probabilities, then they contain the same information. **This point initially confused me: there is the judge LLM (which is giving the masked word probabilities) and then there is the LLM being measured (which gives the distribution summary and real distribution). These are not the same LLM.**

The findings are that the metric is generally more effective than the baselines they show, especially when it comes to nuanced judgements (judging distribution summaries that are subtly wrong in small ways). They also validate that it correlates well with human judgements.

Having established the effectiveness of the metric, they then proceed to measure various LLMs via this metric to see if they can generate effective distribution summaries in a single inference call, and conclude that *they cannot*. Neither simple prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, reasoning models (like DeepSeek-R1), nor finetuning successfully get the LLMs to generate faithful summaries. They state that LLMs are effective at writing good distribution summary strings given samples from the distribution (the "Sample & Summarize" approach), but not at actually "introspecting" and generating the distribution summaries based on their own internal state.

strengths.value:
I think the problem being presented (existing methods like providing a single number representing the certainty of one answer not being rich enough to understand the LLMs internal state) is interesting and well-motivated. 

The metric is validated extensively. I especially appreciate the human study.

The theoretical connection to predictive sufficiency is compelling, the proofs look rigorous.

The authors do seem to have tested the negative result extensively, trying many different approaches to have the models be able to introspect. They establish that "model introspection" is an open and very difficult problem.

Results are comprehensive and reproducible, writing quality in the paper is clear and comprehensive.

weaknesses.value:
I am not sure that the authors effectively justify why a natural language summary of the answer distribution is better than just teaching the model to generate structured output representing is answer distribution: something like [("Paris", 0.75), ("Marseille", 0.15), ("Toulouse", 0.10)].

The example the authors provide in their diagram (Figure 3) is interesting, but it's not at all clear to me what happens when you extrapolate to N=50. What do the summary strings actually look like? Is it an enumeration of 30 different answers in e.g. high variance cases? Is this a useful thing to look at as an end-user? It would be interesting to incorporate some notion of "utility" for an end-user.

What is the "compression strategy" the LLMs are using to generate these distribution summaries? I'm assuming some answers get tossed. Which ones, and why, and are we losing important distributional information this way? It's not clear to me. Like I understand your metric hypothetically should avoid losing important distributional information. But I still really would like to see what the final distribution summaries look like at this level. Appendix E is somewhat informative but not sufficient: it demonstrates the metric, but not what the actual distribution summaries generated from the LLMs look like. 

I think a qualitative analysis of some examples of the summaries generated would be extremely useful.

The paper is extremely dense and long, with the appendices. Some important details are buried in the appendices, it's so long I may have missed other details, not sure.

I think the paper may be overreaching in its claims, specifically regarding the second contribution: examining if LLMs are capable of expressing distributional summaries without access to samples from the distribution, and if they can be trained to do so. "With SelfReflect, we make a resounding negative observation: modern LLMs are, across the board, incapable of revealing what they are uncertain about, neither through reasoning, nor chains-of-thoughts, nor explicit finetuning." -- I think this is slight overclaiming, they are not able to estimate their answer distribution, which is one specific way they can make the user aware of their uncertainty.

questions.value:
I would want to see an Appendix with some qualitative analysis of some examples from the N=50 case. What do these summaries look like?

I would want to see some discussion of if these summaries are actually helpful for an end-user. There is no rigorous discussion of whether distribution summaries in natural language are actually useful, and what the benefit is compared to other ways to summarize the distribution of answers from an LLM.

Can an analysis of summary length vs N be done?

To be honest it feels like especially the sample&summarize method is effectively a form of implicit clustering. Like what I must infer is that the summary is essentially grouping different samples together and assigning some probabilities based on the frequency of certain samples over others. "The negative result shows LLMs can't introspect" why do you think this might be? Is it a training data issue, architectural limitation, or something about how RLHF works? Do you have hypotheses for what would enable introspection?"

How does your Sample & Summarize approach compare to existing methods like Semantic Entropy (Farquhar et al. 2024), which also clusters sampled answers? What's the advantage of natural language output over numerical entropy?

Thank you for your feedback. There are two important takeaways from this contribution: 
1. A simple sample-and-summarize method performs reasonably well for summarizing the models distribution from samples and hence can be a faithful (w.r.t. the reference distribution of independent samples) way of communicating models’ uncertainty.
2. In general, methods that don’t explicitly generate samples cannot be trusted to accurately capture this uncertainty faithfully. At a higher level, this elucidates a difficulty LLMs have with “reflecting” on their own predictive distribution for the original question while trying to produce a summary in a single-decoding.

We are optimistic that future work will uncover ways of obtaining a good summary in a single decoding (ie without drawing samples), and feel this is an important open direction for the field. SelfReflect provides a way to evaluate the success of such attempts, and the sample-and-summarize approach offers a strong baseline.

> Q1: Would masking on sentence level be a valid approximation of SelfReflect?

We tested this; we call this the SR-PMI baseline, described in lines 256-258 and Appendix F.3. We find that this yields a less fine-grained metric than SelfReflect, probably because it loses too much context and increases the noise-to-signal ratio of what responses are possible. The masked-out task which apparently makes the context clearer to the judge. To reduce the amount of computations, we found it better to skip stopwords, or to reduce the number of masked-out tasks (see Appendix B.1 and the new experiments in Appendix B.2).

> Q2: Could there be an alternative to using Wasserstein distance?

Yes, indeed we find that SelfReflect is robust to the choice of the exact distance, as long as it is over the whole vocabulary logit vector. For example, replacing Wasserstein distance with KL distance leads to virtually identical results. We choose the Wasserstein over the KL distance because it generalizes gracefully to settings in which we only have the top-1 word, like in blackbox judge models, in which is reduces to an accuracy (we hinted at this in footnote 2, but have now expanded the discussion in the revised paper).
This graceful generalization is related to the capability of (1-)Wasserstein distance to provide a finite and meaningful measure of divergence in two distributions even when the distributions may have zero or little overlap in their support. In such cases, KL-divergence may explode or need to be capped and JS-divergence may return almost flat metric values which carry no meaningful signal to indicate how much the involved distributions differ.  When we use even simpler distances, like comparing only the log likelihood of the true masked word instead of the whole vector, we observe drops in performance (this is the PR-logl baseline in Tables 1-3).

summary.value:
**Summary**: This paper investigates the problem of communicating uncertainty of the distribution over answers to a question, advocating for the generation of all possible answers and their likelihood when generating an answer to a question (instead of generating the most likely answer and a confidence score). It then proceeds with (1) proposing and validating a metric–**SelfReflect**– to quantify the faithfulness of a summary to a LLMs internal distribution over answer, (2) empirically investigating whether through various prompting techniques LLMs are able to produce such descriptive summaries of their internal distribution.

**Main contributions**:

- Novel paradigm for uncertainty quantification, requiring an answer that is descriptive of the LLM’s internal uncertainty.
- Proposal of a theoretically grounded metric, SelfReflect, that measures faithfulness between a descriptive answer (dubbed *summary*) and the LLM’s internal distribution over answers. 
- Extensive experimentation with 16 popular LLMs across 3 datasets to assess their abilities in generating descriptive summaries of their internal uncertainty either through prompting, finding them to be inapt.

strengths.value:
- Novel contributions for uncertainty quantification in LLMs, offering a fresh perspective on uncertainty quantification and designing new set of metrics and evaluations;
- Proposal of a new metric that is grounded in information theory concepts, such as mutual information.
- Experimental design allows for the controlled assessment of the capabilities of the proposed metric, comparing it against numerous baselines including LLM-as-a-judge approaches.
- Benchmark 10+ models in 3+ datasets (TriviaQA, NaturalQuestions, SimpleQA, MMLU) and 5 different prompting strategies and 2 fine-tuning approaches to assess model’s abilities in generating descriptive summaries.
- Various appendices supporting various analyses and arguments in the paper – e.g., providing a convergence analysis of SelfReflect metric.
- Interesting findings, including the model’s inability (even after SFT or DPO) to provide descriptive summaries of its own internal uncertainty.
- Well-written and well-organized.

> Q6: Could the authors motivate the selection of different models across controlled experiments in Section 4?

We started experiments in Section 4 with Qwen 2.5 7B at the time of conception of the project, since it was one of the best open-weight LLMs available. We then decided to diversify and test the robustness of our results on other LLMs, and aimed to have a range of architectures and providers, thus using Google’s Gemma 3 12B and Microsoft’s Phi-4 14B, and Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B. Some experiments have a cross-test over all combinations of models (such as in Appendix D). In Table 1, we instead tested on multiple datasets and in Table 3, conducted a human user study; in these cases including all model combinations would have been excessive in cost. 

> Q7: Section 5 includes experiments with numerous prompting and fine-tuning strategies. I was wondering if an iterative self-critiquing approach would improve upon simple prompting or “sample and summarize”?

Thanks for the suggestion! We have experimented with multi-step refinements of summaries, where we first ask the model to give a summary and then prompt it again to see if there is any other options. The results were similar to CoT, with the model listing options, but those options deviating from what it is actually uncertain about. Hence, the SelfReflect score also did not improve. We have not run these experiments on all model and dataset combinations yet, which is why we did not include them in the paper. If you are interested, we can run this and include the results.

> Q8: In Section 5.2 the authors suggest that despite fine-tuning and providing examples of descriptive summaries to the models, they seem to be unable to perform the task and that “model memorizes individual summaries rather than learning a general mechanism”. Could this be due to data quality issues (since the data is generated synthetically) and/or hyperparameter tuning?

We do not believe so. After submission, we continued our RL experiments, with additional hyperparameters (Appendix M), by using a 10x larger (still synthetic) train dataset, and by training on human-written summaries from Appendix G. We found that the behavior stays the same. Even on the best hyperparameters, SFT training leads to slow improvements on the train dataset that generalize neither to the (same-dataset) eval set nor to the OOD data. We are thus convinced that at this point, naive fine-tuning only leads to learning the specific examples in and out and does not train the underlying (more complex) mechanism of thinking about the possible solutions and then summarizing them in the LLM. We believe that this “algorithm” might need to be made more explicit for the LLM to learn, similar to how it is in Sample & Summarize. 

> Writing style

Thank you for the suggestions! We now link the Krippendorf Alpha implementation we used (https://github.com/grrrr/krippendorff-alpha/tree/master) and fixed the typos in the revised version. 

> Clarity: What's the intuition behind the reference metric in Section 4.2?

We agree that this may not have been clear in the submitted version. We changed it to the following in the revised version (highlighted in blue): Since MMLU is a multiple-choice dataset, we can sample the LLM multiple times to obtain a simple categorical distribution. We then create summaries that either talk about this distribution (``The answer is most likely C (54% sure), but it could also be B (32% sure) or A (14% sure).'') or that mention the most likely answer only, are overconfident, or give random percentages. This gives a range of different-quality summaries that the benchmark metrics have to tell apart. The categorical setup of MMLU also allows to calculate a reference benchmark metric, namely the Wasserstein distance between the percentages mentioned in the summary and that of the real distribution. This lets us test if the SelfReflect metric and the other baselines agrees with the true distance in this special case. Specifically, we report the rank correlation between them and the reference metric.

As such, evaluating performing the second step with models specifically trained for summarization will not elucidate any new qualitative effects, which is the primary purpose of this paper.
